CHAPTER 38 - MATHEMATICAL REASONING

Introduction

Mathematics is built on careful reasoning. Every theorem we accept must be justified by a valid chain of argument that starts from things already known to be true. Mathematical reasoning is the study of the LANGUAGE and the RULES of such arguments. It teaches us how to form precise statements, how to combine them using logical connectives, how to express "for all" and "there exists", how to turn a claim into an implication and examine its converse and contrapositive, and how to PROVE that a statement is true or DISPROVE it with a single counterexample. This chapter introduces the elements of symbolic logic that underlie all of mathematics.

38.1 STATEMENTS (PROPOSITIONS)

A STATEMENT (or proposition) in logic is a declarative sentence that is either TRUE or FALSE, but not both. The property of being true or false is called its TRUTH VALUE (denoted T or F).

Examples of statements:
 - "The number 7 is prime." (a true statement)
 - "5 is greater than 9." (a false statement)
 - "The sum of the angles of a triangle is 180 degrees." (true)

Sentences that are NOT statements:
 - "Close the door." (a command)
 - "What is your name?" (a question)
 - "How beautiful the garden is!" (an exclamation)
 - "x + 3 = 7." (open sentence - its truth depends on x; not a statement until x is fixed)
 - "This sentence is false." (a paradox - cannot be assigned a consistent truth value)

We usually denote statements by small letters p, q, r, s. For example, we may write p: "2 is an even number." Here p is true.

SIMPLE and COMPOUND statements. A SIMPLE statement contains no other statement as a part and cannot be broken down further. A COMPOUND statement is formed by combining two or more simple statements using words called LOGICAL CONNECTIVES such as "and", "or", "not", "if...then", "if and only if". For instance, "2 is even AND 3 is odd" is a compound statement built from two simple statements.

38.2 LOGICAL CONNECTIVES AND TRUTH TABLES

Connectives allow us to build compound statements. A TRUTH TABLE lists all possible combinations of truth values of the component statements and the resulting truth value of the compound statement.

(a) NEGATION (NOT). The negation of a statement p is "not p", written ~p (read "not p"). It reverses the truth value: if p is true, ~p is false, and vice versa.
   p    ~p
   T    F
   F    T
Example: if p: "Delhi is a city", then ~p: "Delhi is not a city" (or "It is not the case that Delhi is a city").

(b) CONJUNCTION (AND). The conjunction of p and q is "p AND q", written p AND q. It is TRUE only when BOTH p and q are true; otherwise it is false.
   p   q   p AND q
   T   T     T
   T   F     F
   F   T     F
   F   F     F
Example: "2 is even AND 3 is prime" is true because both parts are true.

(c) DISJUNCTION (OR). The disjunction of p and q is "p OR q", written p OR q. In mathematics OR is INCLUSIVE: p OR q is TRUE when AT LEAST ONE of p, q is true; it is false only when both are false.
   p   q   p OR q
   T   T     T
   T   F     T
   F   T     T
   F   F     F
Example: "3 is even OR 3 is odd" is true because the second part is true.

The exclusive OR (either one or the other but not both) is a different connective, used less often, and is not the default meaning in mathematics.

38.3 QUANTIFIERS

Many mathematical statements speak about a whole collection of objects. To express these we use QUANTIFIERS.

(a) The UNIVERSAL quantifier "for all" (symbol: for all, written here as "for all") asserts that a property holds for EVERY member of a set. Example: "for all natural numbers n, n + 0 = n." This is true. A universally quantified statement is FALSE if even ONE member fails the property.

(b) The EXISTENTIAL quantifier "there exists" (written here as "there exists") asserts that a property holds for AT LEAST ONE member. Example: "there exists a natural number n such that n^2 = 9." This is true (n = 3). An existential statement is TRUE if at least one member works, and FALSE only if no member works.

NEGATION OF QUANTIFIED STATEMENTS. The negation of "for all x, P(x)" is "there exists x such that not P(x)". The negation of "there exists x such that P(x)" is "for all x, not P(x)". In words, the negation of "every A is B" is "some A is not B", and the negation of "some A is B" is "no A is B". Example: the negation of "for all real x, x^2 >= 0" would be "there exists a real x such that x^2 < 0" (which is false, so the original is true).

38.4 IMPLICATIONS (CONDITIONAL STATEMENTS)

A CONDITIONAL statement (implication) has the form "if p then q", written p -> q (read "p implies q"). Here p is the HYPOTHESIS (antecedent) and q is the CONCLUSION (consequent). The truth table is:
   p   q   p -> q
   T   T     T
   T   F     F
   F   T     T
   F   F     T
The key point: p -> q is FALSE ONLY when p is true and q is false. When the hypothesis p is false, the implication is regarded as VACUOUSLY TRUE. Example: "If it rains, then the ground is wet." The only way this promise is broken is if it rains (p true) yet the ground is not wet (q false).

Ways to read p -> q: "p implies q"; "if p then q"; "p only if q"; "q if p"; "p is SUFFICIENT for q"; "q is NECESSARY for p".

FROM A CONDITIONAL WE FORM THREE RELATED STATEMENTS:
 - CONVERSE of p -> q is q -> p.
 - INVERSE of p -> q is ~p -> ~q.
 - CONTRAPOSITIVE of p -> q is ~q -> ~p.

Worked example. Let the statement be "If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even" (p -> q).
 - Converse (q -> p): "If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4." (This is FALSE; 6 is even but not divisible by 4.)
 - Inverse (~p -> ~q): "If a number is not divisible by 4, then it is not even." (Also FALSE; 6 is not divisible by 4 yet is even.)
 - Contrapositive (~q -> ~p): "If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 4." (TRUE.)

Two very important facts of logic:
 (1) A conditional and its CONTRAPOSITIVE are LOGICALLY EQUIVALENT - they always have the same truth value: (p -> q) is equivalent to (~q -> ~p).
 (2) The CONVERSE and the INVERSE are logically equivalent to each other, but NEITHER is equivalent to the original conditional. So the truth of p -> q does not guarantee the truth of its converse.

BICONDITIONAL (IF AND ONLY IF). The biconditional "p if and only if q", written p <-> q, means p and q have the SAME truth value. It is equivalent to (p -> q) AND (q -> p). Truth table:
   p   q   p <-> q
   T   T     T
   T   F     F
   F   T     F
   F   F     T
So p <-> q is TRUE exactly when both are true or both are false. Here p is a NECESSARY AND SUFFICIENT condition for q. Example: "A triangle is equilateral if and only if all its angles are equal."

38.5 TAUTOLOGY, CONTRADICTION AND CONTINGENCY

Consider a compound statement built from p, q, ... . Looking at its truth table:
 - A TAUTOLOGY is a compound statement that is TRUE for EVERY assignment of truth values to its components. Example: p OR ~p (the law of the excluded middle) is always true.
 - A CONTRADICTION (or fallacy) is one that is FALSE for every assignment. Example: p AND ~p is always false.
 - A CONTINGENCY is a statement that is true for some assignments and false for others (neither a tautology nor a contradiction). Example: p -> q.

LOGICAL EQUIVALENCE. Two compound statements are LOGICALLY EQUIVALENT (written with the symbol "equiv" or =) if they have IDENTICAL truth tables - the same truth value for every assignment. Equivalently, X and Y are logically equivalent if and only if the biconditional X <-> Y is a tautology. We already met one key equivalence: (p -> q) is equivalent to (~q -> ~p).

Another useful equivalence expresses an implication using OR: (p -> q) is equivalent to (~p OR q). This is easily checked by comparing truth tables.

DE MORGAN'S LAWS (for logic). These describe how negation interacts with AND and OR:
 - ~(p AND q) is equivalent to (~p OR ~q).
 - ~(p OR q) is equivalent to (~p AND ~q).
In words: the negation of a conjunction is the disjunction of the negations, and the negation of a disjunction is the conjunction of the negations. Example: the negation of "It is raining AND it is cold" is "It is not raining OR it is not cold."

Some standard equivalences (laws of logic): commutative laws (p AND q equiv q AND p; p OR q equiv q OR p), associative laws, distributive laws, identity and complement laws, double negation (~(~p) equiv p), and the two De Morgan laws above. All can be verified with truth tables.

38.6 VALIDATING STATEMENTS - METHODS OF PROOF

To VALIDATE a statement means to establish whether it is true (prove it) or false (disprove it). Several standard methods are used.

(1) DIRECT PROOF. To prove p -> q directly, assume p is true and, through a chain of valid logical steps and known facts, deduce that q is true. Example: prove "if n is an even integer, then n^2 is even." Assume n is even, so n = 2k for some integer k. Then n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2), which is even. Hence the statement is proved.

(2) PROOF BY CONTRAPOSITIVE. Since p -> q is logically equivalent to ~q -> ~p, we may prove the contrapositive instead. Example: prove "if n^2 is even, then n is even." Prove the contrapositive: "if n is odd, then n^2 is odd." If n is odd, n = 2k + 1, so n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, which is odd. This proves the contrapositive and hence the original.

(3) PROOF BY CONTRADICTION (reductio ad absurdum). To prove a statement, assume its NEGATION is true and derive a contradiction (something known to be false). The contradiction shows the assumption was wrong, so the original statement is true. The classic example is proving that sqrt(2) is irrational: assume sqrt(2) = a/b in lowest terms; then 2b^2 = a^2, forcing a and b to share a factor of 2, contradicting "lowest terms". Hence sqrt(2) is irrational.

(4) PROOF BY COUNTEREXAMPLE. To DISPROVE a universal statement "for all x, P(x)", it is enough to exhibit ONE value of x for which P(x) is false - a single COUNTEREXAMPLE. Example: to disprove "for all real numbers x, x^2 > x", take x = 1/2; then x^2 = 1/4 which is NOT greater than 1/2. One counterexample settles it. Note that a counterexample can never PROVE a "for all" statement - it can only disprove one.

There is also PROOF BY MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION (used for statements about all natural numbers), but the four methods above are the core techniques of validating statements in this chapter.

A GENERAL STRATEGY: to prove "p if and only if q" you must prove BOTH directions, p -> q and q -> p. To disprove an implication p -> q you must find a case where p is true but q is false.

SUMMARY

- A STATEMENT (proposition) is a declarative sentence that is either true or false but not both; commands, questions, exclamations and open sentences are not statements.
- Simple statements combine, via CONNECTIVES, into compound statements: negation ~p, conjunction p AND q, disjunction p OR q.
- Truth tables: ~p reverses p; p AND q is true only when both are true; p OR q (inclusive) is false only when both are false.
- QUANTIFIERS: "for all" (universal) needs the property for every member; "there exists" (existential) needs it for at least one. Negating swaps the two: not(for all P) = there exists (not P), and not(there exists P) = for all (not P).
- The CONDITIONAL p -> q is false only when p is true and q is false. Its converse is q -> p, inverse is ~p -> ~q, contrapositive is ~q -> ~p.
- A conditional is logically equivalent to its contrapositive; the converse and inverse are equivalent to each other but not to the original.
- The BICONDITIONAL p <-> q is true when p and q have the same truth value; it means (p -> q) AND (q -> p), a necessary and sufficient condition.
- A TAUTOLOGY is always true (e.g. p OR ~p); a CONTRADICTION is always false (e.g. p AND ~p); a CONTINGENCY is sometimes true, sometimes false.
- Two statements are LOGICALLY EQUIVALENT when their truth tables match; e.g. (p -> q) equiv (~p OR q). DE MORGAN'S laws: ~(p AND q) equiv (~p OR ~q) and ~(p OR q) equiv (~p AND ~q).
- METHODS OF PROOF: direct proof, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, and disproof by counterexample; a single counterexample disproves a universal statement.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Mathematical Reasoning (NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. For truth-table problems show every row. State clearly which connective or method you use, and justify your answers.

questions.question: Which of the following are statements? Give the truth value where possible. (a) 7 is a prime number. (b) Close the window. (c) x + 2 = 5. (d) The Sun rises in the west.
questions.answer:
(a) Statement - TRUE (7 is prime).
(b) Not a statement - it is a command.
(c) Not a statement - it is an open sentence; its truth depends on the value of x.
(d) Statement - FALSE (the Sun rises in the east).
questions.explanation: A statement is a declarative sentence that is definitely true or false.

questions.question: Write the negation of each statement: (a) p: 5 is an odd number. (b) q: All triangles are equilateral.
questions.answer:
(a) ~p: 5 is not an odd number (i.e. 5 is even). Since p is true, ~p is false.
(b) ~q: Not all triangles are equilateral, i.e. there exists a triangle that is not equilateral. Since q is false, ~q is true.
questions.explanation: Negation reverses truth value; negation of 'all' is 'some ... not'.

questions.question: Construct the truth table for p AND (~q).
questions.answer:
Columns p, q, ~q, p AND ~q:
p=T, q=T: ~q=F, p AND ~q = F
p=T, q=F: ~q=T, p AND ~q = T
p=F, q=T: ~q=F, p AND ~q = F
p=F, q=F: ~q=T, p AND ~q = F
So p AND ~q is true only in the row p=T, q=F.
questions.explanation: Conjunction is true only when both parts are true.

questions.question: For the statement 'If a number is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by 3', write the converse, inverse and contrapositive, and state the truth value of each.
questions.answer:
Let p: a number is divisible by 6; q: a number is divisible by 3. The statement is p -> q, which is TRUE.
Converse (q -> p): 'If a number is divisible by 3, then it is divisible by 6.' FALSE (9 is divisible by 3 but not by 6).
Inverse (~p -> ~q): 'If a number is not divisible by 6, then it is not divisible by 3.' FALSE (9 is not divisible by 6 but is divisible by 3).
Contrapositive (~q -> ~p): 'If a number is not divisible by 3, then it is not divisible by 6.' TRUE (equivalent to the original).
Note the original and its contrapositive are both true; the converse and inverse are both false.
questions.explanation: Converse q->p, inverse ~p->~q, contrapositive ~q->~p; contrapositive matches original.

questions.question: Show, using a truth table, that p OR ~p is a tautology and p AND ~p is a contradiction.
questions.answer:
For p OR ~p:
p=T: ~p=F, p OR ~p = T
p=F: ~p=T, p OR ~p = T
Always T, so it is a tautology.
For p AND ~p:
p=T: ~p=F, p AND ~p = F
p=F: ~p=T, p AND ~p = F
Always F, so it is a contradiction.
questions.explanation: Excluded middle is always true; contradiction always false.

questions.question: Verify De Morgan's law ~(p AND q) is equivalent to (~p OR ~q) using a truth table.
questions.answer:
Build the table for the four rows:
p=T,q=T: p AND q=T, ~(p AND q)=F; ~p=F,~q=F, ~p OR ~q=F. Match.
p=T,q=F: p AND q=F, ~(p AND q)=T; ~p=F,~q=T, ~p OR ~q=T. Match.
p=F,q=T: p AND q=F, ~(p AND q)=T; ~p=T,~q=F, ~p OR ~q=T. Match.
p=F,q=F: p AND q=F, ~(p AND q)=T; ~p=T,~q=T, ~p OR ~q=T. Match.
The two columns are identical in all rows, so ~(p AND q) equiv (~p OR ~q).
questions.explanation: Identical truth-table columns prove the equivalence.

questions.question: Prove by contradiction that sqrt(2) is irrational.
questions.answer:
Assume the opposite: sqrt(2) is rational. Then sqrt(2) = a/b where a, b are integers with no common factor (fraction in lowest terms) and b is not 0.
Squaring: 2 = a^2 / b^2, so a^2 = 2 b^2. Thus a^2 is even, which forces a to be even; write a = 2c.
Then (2c)^2 = 2 b^2, i.e. 4c^2 = 2 b^2, so b^2 = 2 c^2. Hence b^2 is even and b is even.
But now a and b are both even, so they share the factor 2 - contradicting the assumption that a/b was in lowest terms.
The contradiction shows our assumption was false, so sqrt(2) is irrational.
questions.explanation: Assume rational in lowest terms, derive that both a and b are even - a contradiction.

questions.question: Disprove the statement: 'For all real numbers x, x^2 > x.'
questions.answer: The statement is universal, so one counterexample disproves it. Take x = 1/2. Then x^2 = 1/4, and 1/4 is NOT greater than 1/2. Since the property fails for x = 1/2, the statement 'for all real x, x^2 > x' is false. (Any x with 0 < x < 1, or x = 0 or x = 1, also works as a counterexample.)
questions.explanation: A single counterexample disproves a 'for all' statement.

questions.question: Prove directly: if n is an odd integer, then n^2 is odd.
questions.answer: Assume n is odd, so n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. Then n^2 = (2k + 1)^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1. Since 2k^2 + 2k is an integer, n^2 has the form 2m + 1, which is odd. Hence if n is odd then n^2 is odd.
questions.explanation: Direct proof: substitute n = 2k+1 and simplify to 2m+1.

questions.question: Write the following in symbols using quantifiers, then negate: 'Every natural number is greater than zero.'
questions.answer:
In symbols: for all n (n is a natural number), n > 0. Symbolically, for all n, n > 0.
Negation: there exists a natural number n such that n is NOT greater than 0, i.e. there exists n with n <= 0. (The original statement is true for natural numbers 1, 2, 3, ..., so its negation is false.)
questions.explanation: Negation of 'for all P' is 'there exists not P'.

The second combines two simple statements using 'and'.

questions.question: Write the truth table for the negation connective ~p.
questions.answer:

p = T -> ~p = F

So ~p is true exactly when p is false, and false when p is true.
questions.explanation: Negation flips T and F.

questions.question: Distinguish between the inclusive OR and the exclusive OR, with an example of each.
questions.answer:
Inclusive OR (the mathematical default) p OR q is true when at least one of p, q is true, INCLUDING the case where both are true. Example: 'A student offers Mathematics OR Physics' allows a student taking both.
Exclusive OR is true when exactly one of p, q is true but NOT both. Example: 'The switch is up OR down' - it cannot be both at once. In mathematics OR means the inclusive one unless stated otherwise.
questions.explanation: Inclusive: at least one (both allowed); exclusive: exactly one.

questions.explanation: Only true when p is false and q is true.

questions.question: Using a truth table, show that p -> q and ~p OR q have the same truth values.
questions.answer:
Rows p, q, p -> q, ~p, ~p OR q:

p=T,q=F: p->q=F; ~p=F, ~p OR q=F. Match.

p=F,q=F: p->q=T; ~p=T, ~p OR q=T. Match.

questions.explanation: Identical columns confirm the equivalence.

questions.explanation: Always true; a conjunction implies each of its parts.

questions.question: Write the following using a quantifier and give its truth value: 'The square of every real number is non-negative.'
questions.answer: In symbols: for all real x, x^2 >= 0. This is TRUE, because the square of any real number is either positive or zero, never negative.
questions.explanation: Universal statement, true for all real x.

questions.question: Write the negation of each: (a) for all x, x^2 >= 0. (b) There exists a prime number that is even.
questions.answer:

(b) Negation: for all prime numbers, the number is not even, i.e. no prime is even. (This negation is false, since 2 is an even prime.)
questions.explanation: Negation swaps universal and existential and negates the property.

questions.question: Determine the truth value of 'there exists a natural number n such that n + n = n', and justify.
questions.answer: For natural numbers, n + n = n gives n = 0. Depending on the convention, if 0 is included among the natural numbers then n = 0 satisfies it and the statement is true; if natural numbers start at 1, no n satisfies n + n = n and the statement is false. Taking the usual school convention (naturals begin at 1), there is no such n, so the statement is FALSE.
questions.explanation: Requires n = 0; false if naturals start at 1.

questions.question: State the converse, inverse and contrapositive of the conditional p -> q in symbols.
questions.answer:

Converse: q -> p
Inverse: ~p -> ~q
Contrapositive: ~q -> ~p
The original and the contrapositive are logically equivalent; the converse and inverse are equivalent to each other.

Contrapositive (~q -> ~p): 'If two lines intersect, then they are not parallel.' This is TRUE, and being the contrapositive it has the same truth value as the (true) original statement.
questions.explanation: Contrapositive negates and swaps; equivalent to original.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of 'p is a necessary and sufficient condition for q', and connect it to the biconditional.
questions.answer: 'p is sufficient for q' means p -> q (having p guarantees q). 'p is necessary for q' means q -> p (q cannot hold without p). When BOTH hold, p is a necessary AND sufficient condition for q, which is exactly the biconditional p <-> q: p and q always have the same truth value. Example: 'a triangle is equilateral if and only if all its sides are equal.'
questions.explanation: Necessary and sufficient = biconditional (both implications).

questions.question: Classify (p -> q) OR (q -> p) as a tautology, contradiction or contingency, with reasoning.
questions.answer: Test all rows. In any row at least one of p -> q, q -> p must be true: an implication is false only when its hypothesis is true and conclusion false; p -> q and q -> p cannot both be false simultaneously (that would need p true, q false AND q true, p false). Checking the four rows gives value T every time, so (p -> q) OR (q -> p) is a TAUTOLOGY.
questions.explanation: The two implications cannot both fail, so the disjunction is always true.

questions.question: State De Morgan's laws for logic and give an everyday-language example of the first.
questions.answer:
De Morgan's laws:
~(p AND q) is equivalent to (~p OR ~q).
~(p OR q) is equivalent to (~p AND ~q).
Example of the first: the negation of 'It is sunny AND warm' is 'It is not sunny OR it is not warm.' The negation of a conjunction is the disjunction of the negations.
questions.explanation: Negation distributes over AND/OR, swapping the connective.

questions.question: Show that ~(p -> q) is logically equivalent to p AND ~q.
questions.answer:
Recall p -> q is false only when p is true and q is false, i.e. when p AND ~q is true. So ~(p -> q) is true exactly when p AND ~q is true. Row by row:
p=T,q=T: p->q=T, ~(p->q)=F; p AND ~q=F. Match.
p=T,q=F: p->q=F, ~(p->q)=T; p AND ~q=T. Match.
p=F,q=T: p->q=T, ~(p->q)=F; p AND ~q=F. Match.
p=F,q=F: p->q=T, ~(p->q)=F; p AND ~q=F. Match.
Hence ~(p -> q) equiv (p AND ~q).
questions.explanation: Negating an implication gives 'hypothesis true and conclusion false'.

questions.question: Prove directly that the sum of two even integers is even.
questions.answer: Let the two even integers be a = 2m and b = 2n for integers m and n. Then a + b = 2m + 2n = 2(m + n). Since m + n is an integer, a + b is of the form 2 times an integer, i.e. it is even. Hence the sum of two even integers is even.
questions.explanation: Write evens as 2m, 2n; factor out 2.

questions.question: Disprove: 'For all natural numbers n, n^2 - n + 41 is prime.'
questions.answer: This is a universal statement, so a single counterexample suffices. Take n = 41: then n^2 - n + 41 = 41^2 - 41 + 41 = 41^2 = 1681, which equals 41 x 41 and is NOT prime. So the statement is false. (n = 41 is a valid counterexample.)
questions.explanation: n = 41 gives 41^2, which is composite.

questions.question: Prove by contrapositive: if n^2 is odd, then n is odd (n an integer).
questions.answer: The contrapositive is: 'if n is not odd (i.e. n is even), then n^2 is not odd (i.e. n^2 is even).' Assume n is even, so n = 2k. Then n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2), which is even. This proves the contrapositive, and since a statement is equivalent to its contrapositive, the original 'if n^2 is odd then n is odd' is proved.
questions.explanation: Prove the equivalent contrapositive using n = 2k.

questions.question: A student writes: 'To prove p <-> q I proved p -> q, so the biconditional holds.' Evaluate this argument.
questions.answer: The argument is INCOMPLETE and therefore invalid. A biconditional p <-> q requires BOTH directions: p -> q AND q -> p. Proving only p -> q establishes one direction; the converse q -> p might be false. For example, 'a number divisible by 6 is divisible by 3' is true, but the converse fails, so 'divisible by 6 if and only if divisible by 3' is false. The student must also prove q -> p.
questions.explanation: A biconditional needs both implications proved.

questions.question: Evaluate whether the following is a valid disproof: 'The statement for all real x, x^2 >= x is false because x = 3 gives 9 >= 3, which is true.'
questions.answer: The disproof is INVALID. To disprove a 'for all' statement one must exhibit a value where the property FAILS, i.e. where x^2 < x. The value x = 3 gives 9 >= 3, which SATISFIES the property and so is not a counterexample; supporting instances cannot disprove a universal claim. (In fact a genuine counterexample is x = 1/2, giving 1/4 < 1/2, but note the original claim with >= is actually true for all real x, so it cannot be disproved.)
questions.explanation: A confirming case is not a counterexample.

questions.question: Which proof method is most suitable to show that there is no largest prime number, and why?
questions.answer: Proof by CONTRADICTION is most suitable. Assume there IS a largest prime; list all primes up to it, multiply them and add 1. The new number is either prime or has a prime factor not in the list, in both cases giving a prime larger than the assumed largest - a contradiction. So no largest prime exists. The method fits because the claim is a non-existence/negative statement naturally handled by assuming the opposite.
questions.explanation: Contradiction suits non-existence claims (Euclid's argument).

questions.question: Explain what is meant by a statement in mathematical logic. Give two examples of sentences that ARE statements and two that are NOT, with reasons.
questions.answer:
A STATEMENT (proposition) in mathematical logic is a declarative sentence that is definitely either TRUE or FALSE, but not both at the same time. Its true/false label is its truth value.

Sentences that ARE statements:
(1) '11 is a prime number.' - declarative and true, so a statement (truth value T).
(2) 'The square of 3 is 8.' - declarative and false, so a statement (truth value F).

Sentences that are NOT statements:
(1) 'Please open your books.' - a command; it is neither true nor false.
(2) 'x - 2 = 5.' - an open sentence; its truth depends on x (true for x = 7, false otherwise), so it has no fixed truth value until x is specified.
Questions ('What is the time?') and exclamations ('How nice!') are also not statements for the same reason - they carry no truth value.
questions.explanation: Definition + two valid statements + two non-statements with reasons.

questions.question: Define the three basic connectives negation, conjunction and disjunction, and give the truth table of each.
questions.answer:
NEGATION (~p): reverses the truth value of p.
p=T -> ~p=F; p=F -> ~p=T.

CONJUNCTION (p AND q): true only when both p and q are true.
p=T,q=T -> T; p=T,q=F -> F; p=F,q=T -> F; p=F,q=F -> F.

DISJUNCTION (p OR q), inclusive: true when at least one of p, q is true; false only when both are false.
p=T,q=T -> T; p=T,q=F -> T; p=F,q=T -> T; p=F,q=F -> F.

Thus AND is the most demanding (needs both true), OR is the most lenient (needs one true), and NOT simply flips a single statement.
questions.explanation: Three definitions with complete truth tables.

questions.question: Construct the complete truth table for the compound statement (p -> q) AND (q -> p), and hence identify the connective it represents.
questions.answer:
We build columns for p, q, p -> q, q -> p, and the conjunction (p -> q) AND (q -> p).
Row 1: p=T, q=T: p->q=T, q->p=T, conjunction = T.
Row 2: p=T, q=F: p->q=F, q->p=T, conjunction = F.
Row 3: p=F, q=T: p->q=T, q->p=F, conjunction = F.
Row 4: p=F, q=F: p->q=T, q->p=T, conjunction = T.
The compound statement is TRUE exactly when p and q have the SAME truth value (both T or both F) and false when they differ. This is precisely the truth table of the BICONDITIONAL p <-> q. Hence (p -> q) AND (q -> p) is logically equivalent to p <-> q.
questions.explanation: Four-row table; result matches the biconditional.

questions.question: Explain the universal and existential quantifiers. State the rule for negating quantified statements and illustrate with one example of each.
questions.answer:
The UNIVERSAL quantifier 'for all' claims a property holds for EVERY member of a set. Example: 'for all integers n, n + 0 = n' - true. Such a statement is false if even one member fails.
The EXISTENTIAL quantifier 'there exists' claims a property holds for AT LEAST ONE member. Example: 'there exists an integer n such that n^2 = 25' - true (n = 5 or -5). It is false only if no member works.

RULES FOR NEGATION:
not(for all x, P(x)) = there exists x such that not P(x).
not(there exists x, P(x)) = for all x, not P(x).
Examples:
(1) Negation of 'for all real x, x^2 >= 0' is 'there exists a real x with x^2 < 0' (which is false, matching that the original is true).
(2) Negation of 'there exists a natural number that is negative' is 'every natural number is non-negative' (true, matching that the original is false).
questions.explanation: Both quantifiers, the two negation rules, and worked examples.

questions.question: Take the statement 'If a triangle is equilateral, then it is isosceles.' Write its converse, inverse, contrapositive and biconditional, and discuss the truth value of each.
questions.answer:
Let p: a triangle is equilateral; q: a triangle is isosceles. The statement is p -> q, which is TRUE (an equilateral triangle, having all sides equal, certainly has two equal sides).
CONVERSE (q -> p): 'If a triangle is isosceles, then it is equilateral.' FALSE - an isosceles triangle may have only two equal sides.
INVERSE (~p -> ~q): 'If a triangle is not equilateral, then it is not isosceles.' FALSE - a triangle can be non-equilateral yet isosceles.
CONTRAPOSITIVE (~q -> ~p): 'If a triangle is not isosceles, then it is not equilateral.' TRUE - equivalent to the original.
BICONDITIONAL (p <-> q): 'A triangle is equilateral if and only if it is isosceles.' FALSE, because although p -> q is true, the converse q -> p is false, and a biconditional needs both directions.
Summary: the original and contrapositive are true; the converse and inverse are false; the biconditional is false.
questions.explanation: All four related statements plus the biconditional with truth values.

questions.question: Using truth tables, prove the distributive law p AND (q OR r) is equivalent to (p AND q) OR (p AND r).
questions.answer:
We need all 8 rows for p, q, r. Compute LHS = p AND (q OR r) and RHS = (p AND q) OR (p AND r).
p=T,q=T,r=T: qORr=T, LHS=T; pANDq=T, pANDr=T, RHS=T.
p=T,q=T,r=F: qORr=T, LHS=T; pANDq=T, pANDr=F, RHS=T.
p=T,q=F,r=T: qORr=T, LHS=T; pANDq=F, pANDr=T, RHS=T.
p=T,q=F,r=F: qORr=F, LHS=F; pANDq=F, pANDr=F, RHS=F.
p=F,q=T,r=T: LHS = F AND T = F; pANDq=F, pANDr=F, RHS=F.
p=F,q=T,r=F: LHS=F; RHS=F.
p=F,q=F,r=T: LHS=F; RHS=F.
p=F,q=F,r=F: LHS=F; RHS=F.
The LHS and RHS columns agree in all 8 rows, so p AND (q OR r) is logically equivalent to (p AND q) OR (p AND r). This is the distributive law of AND over OR.
questions.explanation: Eight-row truth table with matching LHS and RHS columns.

questions.question: Describe the four main methods of validating statements (direct proof, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, counterexample), giving a short worked illustration of each.
questions.answer:
(1) DIRECT PROOF: assume the hypothesis p and deduce q. Illustration - 'if n is even then n^2 is even': let n = 2k, then n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2), even.
(2) PROOF BY CONTRAPOSITIVE: prove ~q -> ~p, which is equivalent to p -> q. Illustration - 'if n^2 is even then n is even': prove 'if n is odd then n^2 is odd' using n = 2k+1 so n^2 = 2(2k^2+2k)+1, odd.
(3) PROOF BY CONTRADICTION: assume the statement is false and derive an absurdity. Illustration - 'sqrt(2) is irrational': assuming sqrt(2)=a/b in lowest terms leads to a and b both even, contradicting 'lowest terms'.
(4) COUNTEREXAMPLE: to disprove a universal statement, exhibit one failing case. Illustration - 'for all real x, x^2 > x' is disproved by x = 1/2 since 1/4 is not greater than 1/2.
Direct, contrapositive and contradiction PROVE a statement; a counterexample only DISPROVES a universal one.
questions.explanation: Four methods each with a concise illustration.

questions.question: A claim states: 'For every pair of integers a and b, if a b is even then a is even.' Decide whether the claim is true, and justify by either proving it or disproving it, explaining the method you chose.
questions.answer:
The claim is FALSE. It is a universal statement, so a single counterexample disproves it. Take a = 3 (odd) and b = 2 (even). Then a b = 6, which is even, yet a = 3 is NOT even. So the hypothesis 'a b is even' holds while the conclusion 'a is even' fails - a genuine counterexample.
Method and reasoning: because the statement is of the form 'for all a, b, ...', the correct way to REFUTE it is by counterexample, not by proof. The true statement in this area is weaker: 'if a b is even, then a is even OR b is even' (at least one factor must be even). Our example respects this - b is even - which is exactly why a is free to be odd. Hence the given claim is disproved, and choosing a counterexample was the appropriate validation method.
questions.explanation: Disproof by counterexample a=3, b=2; explains why counterexample is the right method.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In logic a statement (proposition) is a declarative sentence that is definitely true or definitely false, but not both. Commands, questions, exclamations and open sentences (whose truth depends on a variable) are not statements. Statements are denoted p, q, r and combined by connectives into compound statements.
(a) Give the defining property of a statement.
(b) Is 'x + 4 = 10' a statement? Why or why not?
(c) Classify '3 is odd and 4 is even' as simple or compound.
(d) Write one example each of a sentence that is a statement and one that is not.
questions.answer:
(a) A statement is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both; it has a definite truth value.
(b) No. 'x + 4 = 10' is an open sentence: its truth depends on x (true for x = 6, false otherwise), so it has no fixed truth value and is not a statement.
(c) Compound - it joins the two simple statements '3 is odd' and '4 is even' with the connective 'and'.
(d) Statement: '7 is a prime number' (true). Not a statement: 'Please be quiet.' (a command).
questions.explanation: Definition; open sentence; compound; examples.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The connectives are negation (~p, reverses truth), conjunction (p AND q, true only when both are true) and disjunction (p OR q, inclusive, false only when both are false). Let p: 'It is raining' and q: 'It is cold', with p true and q false.
(a) State the truth value of ~q.
(b) Find the truth value of p AND q.
(c) Find the truth value of p OR q.
(d) Write the compound statement ~p AND q in words and give its truth value.
questions.answer:
(a) q is false, so ~q is TRUE.
(b) p AND q: p is true, q is false, so the conjunction is FALSE (both must be true).
(c) p OR q: p is true, so the disjunction is TRUE (at least one is true).
(d) ~p AND q: 'It is not raining and it is cold.' Here ~p is false (since p is true) and q is false, so the conjunction is FALSE.
questions.explanation: Apply the truth tables to specific values.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A truth table lists every combination of truth values of the component statements and the resulting value of the compound statement. For n statements there are 2^n rows. Consider the compound statement S = (p AND ~q).
(a) How many rows does the truth table of S have?
(b) In which row(s) is S true?
(c) Is S a tautology, contradiction or contingency?
(d) Write a compound statement, using p and q, that is a contradiction.
questions.answer:
(a) Two statements p and q give 2^2 = 4 rows.
(b) S = p AND ~q is true only when p is true and ~q is true, i.e. p=T and q=F - the single row (T, F).
(c) Since S is true in one row and false in the other three, it is a CONTINGENCY (neither always true nor always false).
(d) A contradiction using p and q is, for example, p AND ~p (always false); another is (p AND q) AND ~p.
questions.explanation: Rows, true-row, classification, and a contradiction example.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The universal quantifier 'for all' claims a property for every member of a set; the existential quantifier 'there exists' claims it for at least one. Negation swaps them: not(for all x, P) = there exists x, not P; not(there exists x, P) = for all x, not P.
(a) Name the quantifier in 'Every integer has a successor'.
(b) Write 'Some real numbers are irrational' using a quantifier.
(c) Write the negation of 'for all n, n^2 >= n' (n a natural number).
(d) Is 'there exists an even prime number' true or false? Justify.
questions.answer:
(a) The universal quantifier 'for all' ('every').
(b) There exists a real number x such that x is irrational.
(c) Negation: there exists a natural number n such that n^2 < n. (This negation is false, since n^2 >= n holds for all natural numbers.)
(d) TRUE. The number 2 is prime and even, so at least one even prime exists.
questions.explanation: Identify quantifier; symbolise; negate; evaluate existential.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
For a conditional p -> q, the converse is q -> p, the inverse is ~p -> ~q and the contrapositive is ~q -> ~p. A conditional and its contrapositive are logically equivalent. Consider: 'If a number is divisible by 10, then it is divisible by 5.'
(a) Identify p and q.
(b) Write the contrapositive and state its truth value.
(c) Write the converse and state its truth value.
(d) Are the original and the converse both necessarily true? Explain.
questions.answer:
(a) p: a number is divisible by 10; q: a number is divisible by 5. The statement p -> q is true.
(b) Contrapositive (~q -> ~p): 'If a number is not divisible by 5, then it is not divisible by 10.' TRUE (equivalent to the original).
(c) Converse (q -> p): 'If a number is divisible by 5, then it is divisible by 10.' FALSE (15 is divisible by 5 but not by 10).
(d) No. The original is true and so is its contrapositive, but the converse need not be true - here it is false. The truth of a conditional does not guarantee the truth of its converse.
questions.explanation: Converse can differ in truth value from the original.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A tautology is always true, a contradiction always false and a contingency sometimes each. Two statements are logically equivalent when their truth tables match. De Morgan's laws: ~(p AND q) equiv (~p OR ~q) and ~(p OR q) equiv (~p AND ~q).
(a) Classify p OR ~p.
(b) Classify p AND ~p.
(c) Use De Morgan's law to write the negation of 'x > 0 AND x < 10'.
(d) Are p -> q and its contrapositive logically equivalent? How would you check?
questions.answer:
(a) p OR ~p is a TAUTOLOGY (always true - the law of the excluded middle).
(b) p AND ~p is a CONTRADICTION (always false).
(c) By De Morgan, ~(x > 0 AND x < 10) is (x is not > 0) OR (x is not < 10), i.e. x <= 0 OR x >= 10.
(d) Yes, they are logically equivalent. Check by building the truth tables of p -> q and ~q -> ~p; both give the column T, F, T, T, so the tables match.
questions.explanation: Classify; apply De Morgan; verify equivalence by truth tables.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Statements are validated by direct proof (assume p, deduce q), proof by contrapositive (prove ~q -> ~p), proof by contradiction (assume the negation, reach an absurdity) and disproof by counterexample (one failing case).
(a) Which method disproves a 'for all' statement?
(b) Give a counterexample to 'for all primes p, p is odd'.
(c) Outline a direct proof that the product of two odd numbers is odd.
(d) Which method would you use to prove sqrt(3) is irrational?
questions.answer:
(a) A counterexample - a single case where the universal statement fails.
(b) The prime 2 is even, so 'for all primes p, p is odd' is false; p = 2 is a counterexample.
(c) Let the odds be 2m+1 and 2n+1. Their product is (2m+1)(2n+1) = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1, which is of the form 2k+1, hence odd.
(d) Proof by contradiction: assume sqrt(3) = a/b in lowest terms, square to get a^2 = 3b^2, deduce 3 divides both a and b, contradicting 'lowest terms'.
questions.explanation: Match methods to tasks; counterexample; direct proof; contradiction.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
To prove p -> q one may use a direct, contrapositive or contradiction argument; to disprove it one finds a case where p is true and q is false. To prove a biconditional both directions must be shown. A universal statement cannot be proved by a single example.
(a) A student disproves 'for all x, x^2 >= 2x' by trying x = 5. Is this valid?
(b) Give a correct counterexample to that statement.
(c) To prove 'n is even if and only if n^2 is even', what must be shown?
(d) Why can one example never prove a 'for all' statement?
questions.answer:
(a) No. x = 5 gives 25 >= 10, which SATISFIES the inequality, so it is not a counterexample; a confirming case cannot disprove the statement.
(b) A correct counterexample is x = 1: then x^2 = 1 and 2x = 2, and 1 >= 2 is false. (Any 0 < x < 2 works.)
(c) Both directions: 'if n is even then n^2 is even' AND 'if n^2 is even then n is even'.
(d) Because a universal claim asserts the property for EVERY member; one confirming example leaves infinitely many other cases untested, so it cannot establish the general truth.
questions.explanation: Evaluate a flawed disproof; give a real counterexample; biconditional needs both directions.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The biconditional p <-> q ('p if and only if q') is true exactly when p and q have the same truth value, and it means (p -> q) AND (q -> p). Here p is a necessary and sufficient condition for q.
(a) When is p <-> q false?
(b) Express p <-> q using two conditionals.
(c) Is 'a triangle is equilateral if and only if all its angles are equal' true?
(d) If p -> q is true but q -> p is false, what is the truth value of p <-> q?
questions.answer:
(a) p <-> q is false when p and q have DIFFERENT truth values (one true and the other false).
(b) p <-> q is (p -> q) AND (q -> p).
(c) TRUE. A triangle has all sides equal if and only if all its angles are equal (both directions hold), so the biconditional is true.
(d) FALSE. The biconditional needs both directions; since q -> p fails, (p -> q) AND (q -> p) is false.
questions.explanation: Biconditional truth conditions and necessary-and-sufficient meaning.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Logical equivalences let us rewrite statements: (p -> q) equiv (~p OR q); double negation ~(~p) equiv p; De Morgan's laws relate negation to AND and OR. Equivalent statements share the same truth table.
(a) Rewrite p -> q without the -> connective.
(b) Simplify ~(~p).
(c) Rewrite ~(p OR q) using De Morgan's law.
(d) Explain how you would confirm two statements are logically equivalent.
questions.answer:
(a) p -> q is equivalent to ~p OR q.
(b) ~(~p) is equivalent to p (double negation).
(c) ~(p OR q) is equivalent to ~p AND ~q.
(d) Construct the truth tables of both statements over all combinations of the component truth values; if the final columns are identical in every row, the statements are logically equivalent (equivalently, their biconditional is a tautology).
questions.explanation: Rewrite implication; double negation; De Morgan; equivalence test.
